generic: Human Premixed Insulin (biphasic isophane insulin, e.g. 70/30 or 50/50)
cls: Antidiabetic - premixed (biphasic) human insulin combining short-acting (soluble/regular) and intermediate-acting (isophane/NPH) insulin
pharm: A fixed-ratio suspension of soluble (regular) human insulin and isophane (NPH) human insulin providing both prandial and basal glucose-lowering from a single injection
quick: Individualised; typically given twice daily before breakfast and the evening meal, titrated to glucose targets
Inject about 15-30 minutes before a meal (soluble component); eat reliably to avoid hypoglycaemia
Insulin is the treatment of choice for diabetes in pregnancy; dose adjusted as requirements change
Compatible with breastfeeding; requirements may fall - watch for hypoglycaemia
Insulin requirements often fall in renal impairment - monitor and reduce dose as needed
Requirements may fall in hepatic impairment - monitor glucose and adjust
Can cause delayed hypoglycaemia - take with food and monitor
Blood glucose, HbA1c, injection sites, hypoglycaemia and potassium
summary: Human premixed (biphasic) insulin is a fixed-ratio suspension combining soluble (regular) human insulin with isophane (NPH) human insulin - commonly in ratios such as 70/30, 50/50 or 25/75 (soluble shown as the first number in some conventions). It supplies a rapid component to cover meals and an intermediate component for background needs from a single subcutaneous injection, and is used for diabetes mellitus when a simpler regimen than separate basal-bolus injections is preferred, typically given twice daily before the morning and evening meals. Doses are fully individualised and titrated to glucose targets; the main hazard is hypoglycaemia, and meals must be taken reliably after dosing. As an exact data-set entry 'Human Premix' is a group/category descriptor for human premixed insulin rather than a single brand, and the specific product strength and ratio (e.g. units/mL and soluble:isophane ratio) must be confirmed before use.
indications: Diabetes mellitus requiring insulin (type 1 and type 2) where a premixed regimen is appropriate
Maintenance glycaemic control with twice-daily injections covering meals and background needs

dosage.d: Individualised; often started at a low total daily dose and split, e.g. two-thirds before breakfast and one-third before the evening meal
dosage.t: Subcutaneously, usually twice daily before meals

dosage.d: Individualised total daily insulin divided into premixed injections
dosage.n: Basal-bolus may give finer control; premix is a simpler alternative

dosage.d: Adjust by a few units at a time based on glucose monitoring
dosage.n: Account for illness, activity, renal/hepatic changes and pregnancy

admin: Resuspend gently before each dose - roll/tip the vial or pen until uniformly cloudy/milky (do NOT shake vigorously)
Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen, thigh, buttock or upper arm; rotate sites to avoid lipohypertrophy
Give about 15-30 minutes before the meal (regular/soluble component) and ensure the patient eats
Never administer intravenously; premixed/isophane insulins are for subcutaneous use only
Match syringe/pen to the insulin strength (e.g. U-100) and never mix premix with other insulins in the same syringe
Store unopened insulin refrigerated; in-use vials/pens may be kept at room temperature for the labelled period - do not freeze
moa: Insulin binds the insulin receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells, triggering tyrosine-kinase signalling that promotes cellular glucose uptake (via GLUT4 translocation), glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis, while suppressing hepatic glucose output, lipolysis and ketogenesis - lowering blood glucose. In a biphasic preparation the soluble (regular) fraction acts rapidly to cover the post-meal glucose rise, while the isophane (NPH, protamine-complexed) fraction dissolves slowly to provide a longer, intermediate-duration background effect, giving a dual time-action profile from one injection.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to the insulin product or its excipients (e.g. protamine, metacresol)
relative: Variable/unreliable meal intake (premix needs consistent meals)
Intercurrent illness, vomiting or fasting (adjust dose)

preg: Insulin is the preferred treatment for diabetes during pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta appreciably. Requirements typically rise through pregnancy and fall sharply after delivery; doses must be adjusted frequently with close glucose monitoring to avoid both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia.
lact: Insulin is compatible with breastfeeding and is not orally active in the infant. Maternal insulin requirements may decrease during lactation, so monitor for hypoglycaemia and adjust the dose.
renal: Insulin clearance is reduced in renal impairment, so insulin requirements often fall and the risk of hypoglycaemia rises. Monitor glucose closely and reduce the dose as needed.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment can reduce gluconeogenesis and insulin clearance, lowering insulin requirements. Monitor glucose and adjust the dose carefully.

major: Other glucose-lowering agents (sulfonylureas, other insulins) - additive hypoglycaemia risk; adjust doses
Non-selective beta-blockers - can mask warning signs of hypoglycaemia and impair recovery
moderate: Corticosteroids, thiazides, atypical antipsychotics, sympathomimetics - raise blood glucose and increase insulin needs
ACE inhibitors, MAO inhibitors, salicylates, fibrates - may enhance the glucose-lowering effect
Thyroid hormones, oestrogens/oral contraceptives - may alter insulin requirements
minor: Pioglitazone with insulin - increased risk of fluid retention/heart failure
interactions.food: Take in a fixed relationship to meals; carbohydrate intake must match the dose to avoid hypoglycaemia
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol can cause delayed and prolonged hypoglycaemia; consume only with food and monitor glucose
interactions.diagnostics: Causes hypoglycaemia; can lower serum potassium; affects glucose and HbA1c monitoring

common: Transient blurred vision at start of therapy
emergency: Severe hypoglycaemia - give oral fast-acting carbohydrate if able, or IM glucagon / IV glucose if unable
Diabetic ketoacidosis or marked hyperglycaemia from omitted/inadequate dosing

monitoring: Self-monitored capillary blood glucose, with dose titration
Serum potassium where relevant; weight and blood pressure
counsel: Gently mix the cloudy insulin until evenly milky before each dose - do not shake hard, and do not use it if it stays lumpy or clear
Inject under the skin and then eat your meal within about 15-30 minutes; do not skip meals after dosing
Always carry fast sugar (glucose tablets/juice) and know the signs of a low: shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion
Rotate injection sites to prevent fatty lumps that affect absorption
Check your blood sugar as advised; illness, alcohol, exercise and missed meals change your needs
Store spare insulin in the fridge (do not freeze); the pen/vial in use can stay at room temperature for the labelled time
pk: Soluble component about 30 minutes; overall onset within ~30 min of subcutaneous injection
Biphasic - an early peak from the soluble fraction (~2-4 h) and a broader peak from the isophane fraction
Variable; action is governed by the suspension/absorption profile rather than a simple plasma half-life
Intermediate overall - typically up to about 16-24 hours depending on the ratio and dose
Unopened: refrigerate 2-8 C; in use: room temperature for the labelled period (often up to ~28 days); do NOT freeze; protect from heat/light
pearls: 'Human Premix' is a group/category label for premixed (biphasic) HUMAN insulin (e.g. 70/30, 50/50) - confirm the exact strength and soluble:isophane ratio and product before use
Resuspend gently until uniformly cloudy before every dose; never give a premixed/isophane insulin intravenously
Needs reliable, timed meals - hypoglycaemia is the main risk; counsel on recognition and treatment
Requirements fall in renal/hepatic impairment and during lactation, and change through pregnancy - titrate carefully
Distinct from analogue premixes (e.g. lispro/aspart mixes) - human premix uses regular + NPH human insulin and is dosed ~15-30 min before meals
missed: If a premixed dose is missed, do not double the next dose. Check your blood glucose; for a recently missed dose around a meal, follow your clinician's plan (sometimes a reduced dose with food). If unsure, monitor glucose and seek advice rather than guessing.
overdose: Insulin overdose causes hypoglycaemia, which can be severe (confusion, seizures, coma) and prolonged. Treat mild hypoglycaemia with oral fast-acting carbohydrate; for severe cases give intramuscular/subcutaneous glucagon or intravenous dextrose, then provide longer-acting carbohydrate and monitor glucose and potassium closely until stable.
